cases.substantive_issue: Whether respondent no. 1 sublet, assigned, or otherwise parted with possession of the tenanted shop to respondent no. 2 (his son) without the landlord's written consent, where the son was operating the shop but the tenant claimed continuing proprietorship and control.

issue_refs.quote: Thus, the limited point involved here in this petition filed cite8†u/s. 14 (1) (b) that whether the respondent no. 1 has subletted the premises to respondent no. 2 and whether the act alleged by the petitioner amounts to subletting or not.

application_refs.quote: The petitioner, however, has not place on record any documentary proof in this regard except his oral evidence, which is the matter of record.

Respondent, on the other hand, have shown by way of certain documents that since the inception of tenancy one printing press is still being run at the shop in question. The said proprietorship concern is still existing in the name of the respondent no. 1. This fact is not disputed by the petitioner also.
Respondents have further shown by way of some documents that the business in the premises is still in the name of S.R. Printers for which respondent no. 1 is proprietor.

In these circumstances, therefore, I am of the considered opinion that in the light of the above mentioned reasonings and relying upon above mentioned judgment, the petitioner has not been able to show that respondent no. 1 has subletted the tenanted premises to respondent no. 2.

cases.law_scope: Delhi Rent Control Act, Section 14(1)(b), in a Delhi High Court supervisory challenge to the ARCT judgment.
cases.target_stage: Delhi High Court decision in CM(M) 642/2010 reviewing the ARCT judgment under supervisory jurisdiction.
cases.target_court: Delhi High Court, Hon'ble Ms. Justice Indermeet Kaur.
cases.substantive_issue: Whether Mohan Lal had sublet, assigned, or otherwise parted with possession of the premises to his son Anand Parkash under Section 14(1)(b), despite evidence that the premises had been taken for the son's business from inception and the original tenant allegedly retained supervisory control.

issue_refs.quote: seeking eviction of the tenant Shanti Devi (legal heirs of the original tenant) under cite10†Section 14 (1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act (DRCA) had been dismissed.

It is well settled that to make out a case for sub-letting or parting with possession, it means giving of possession to persons other than those to whom the possession had been given by the original lessor and that parted with possession must have been made by the tenant.

application_refs.quote: This finding of the RCT is not only contrary to his own observation and finding returned in the earlier part of the paragraph but is also contrary to the record; it is clearly perverse.

the ARC had returned a correct and cogent finding that the premises had been taken on rent by Mohan Lal for the business of his son Anand Parkash and as such the question of parting with possession/assigning/subletting by Mohan Lal in favour of his son Anand Parkash in this factual scenario did not arise.
In this scenario this finding returned by the RCT is a gross illegality bordering on perversity; it has to be set aside.

Although Mohan Lal was himself not carrying on any CM (M) No. 642/2010 Page 15 of 21 business from the said premises yet it is apparent that he had complete supervisory control over this business which was being run by Anand Parkash for which purpose premises had been taken on rent by Mohan Lal.
Ground under cite10†Section 14(1)(b) of the DRCA was clearly not established

allowed_spans.quote: contention was that the tenant Mohan Lal has sublet these premises to Anand Parkash and others including 'Parkash Trading Corporation' through Ram Parkash
allowed_spans.reason: Landlord's pre-target notice allegation identifying the alleged subletting.

allowed_spans.quote: this contention was denied; stand of the tenant was that the premises in question had been taken on rent by Mohan Lal only for his son Anand Parkash and this was with the consent of the landlord who was living in the same premises and who was fully aware of the fact that Anand Parkash is carrying on the business from the said premises; there was no subletting.
allowed_spans.reason: Tenant's reply gives the competing account that the son's business use existed from inception with the landlord's knowledge.

allowed_spans.quote: AW-4 had proved the electricity connection in the name of Mohan Lal; rent receipt was also in favour of Mohan Lal.
allowed_spans.reason: Documentary evidence tying utilities/rent documentation to Mohan Lal.

allowed_spans.quote: AW-5 had proved the telephone record to show that M/s Parkash Trading Corporation had a telephone installed in the disputed premises up to 21.05.1963 whereafter the firm was dissolved and the telephone was thereafter shifted from the said premises.
allowed_spans.reason: Documentary record of the third-party firm's presence and later dissolution/telephone shift.

allowed_spans.quote: Partnership deed of M/s Parkash Trading Corporation Ex. RW-5/X13 was proved substantiating the averment that Anand Parkash was a partner in the said firm; thereafter this firm was dissolved and another partnership deed was executed Ex.RW-5/X15.
allowed_spans.reason: Rent-receipt counterfoils and partnership deeds were part of the pre-target documentary record.

allowed_spans.quote: it was the deceased Mohan Lal who was the tenant in the premises but since Anand Parkash was carrying on business in these premises from the very beginning which was also admitted by the landlord, no inference of parting with possession/subletting/assignment by Mohan Lal in favour of Anand Parkash could be made
allowed_spans.reason: Prior fact-finding by the ARC on the same subletting issue.

allowed_spans.quote: he had parted with possession of the premises in favour of his son Anand Parkash who was carrying on business in the same premises; ground of subletting under cite10†Section 14 (1)(b) stood confirmed in favour of the landlord.
allowed_spans.reason: Contrary prior finding by the ARCT, preserving the factual-adjudicative variation later reviewed by the target court.

allowed_spans.quote: The landlord Maheshwar Dayal had been examined as AW-7 wherein in his cross-examination he has admitted that Mohan Lal had taken the premises for the business of his son Anand Parkash; further that Anand Parkash right from the inception of the tenancy was using these premises.
allowed_spans.reason: The landlord's cross-examination admission, quoted in the target judgment, is a pre-target evidentiary fact.

cases.law_scope: Delhi Rent Control Act, Section 14(1)(b), with Section 14(4) expressly discussed for the partnership/camouflage question.
cases.target_stage: Delhi High Court decision in CM(M) No.1574/2010 reviewing the ARCT order dated 05.07.2000.
cases.target_court: Delhi High Court, Hon'ble Ms. Justice Indermeet Kaur.
cases.substantive_issue: Whether the tenant's son-in-law occupied the shop under a genuine partnership/assistance arrangement while the tenant retained legal possession, or whether the partnership was a sham device amounting to subletting or parting with possession under Section 14(1)(b) and Section 14(4).

issue_refs.quote: The impugned judgment had reversed this finding noting that a ground of subletting under cite12†Section 14(1)(b) of the DRCA has not been made out.

For the purpose of clause (b) of the proviso to sub-section (1), any premises which have been let for being used for the purposes of business or profession shall be deemed to have been sub-let by the tenant, if the Controller is satisfied that the tenant without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord has, after the 16th day of August, 1958, allowed any person to occupy the whole or any part of the premises ostensibly on the ground that such person is a partner of the tenant in the business or profession but really for the purpose of sub-letting such premises to that person.

application_refs.quote: In this scenario the RCT had correctly appreciated the evidence adduced; it is clear that the son-in-law has come to Delhi to assist his father-in-law in his business in the shop; both were residing in the same premises; because the father-in-law has become very old and because of his old age and weak eyesight he could not come regularly to his shop; his wife Sumitra Devi was opening and closing the shop with her son-in-law; she was also sitting in the shop; Ex.AW-3/13 was in fact not a sham document;
The partnership between the father-in-law and son-in-law is a genuine transaction; it was not a camouflage to cover the real aspect of subletting

Applying the said test to the facts of the instant case, it can safely be said that both the Courts below had returned correct findings in view of the evidence adduced before them ; that a case of sub-letting was not made out.

In fact from the evidence on record, it is clear that Hakim Rai has in no manner had given the possession of the shop in question exclusively to Raj Kumar thereby divesting himself; mere occupation of Raj Kumar in the suit premises was not sufficient to establish a case of subletting as has rightly been noted in the impugned order.

allowed_spans.quote: The case of the petitioner was that a shop on the ground floor of property bearing no.95, Main Bazar, Najafgarh, Delhi which had been let out to the original tenant Hakim Rai and which had since been sublet by him in favour of his son-in-law Raj Kumar; Hakim Rai had divested himself completely from the suit property.
allowed_spans.reason: Landlord's pleaded account of complete divestment and subletting to the son-in-law.

allowed_spans.quote: The defence set up by Hakim Rai (tenant) was that he was old, aged, ailing and had lost his eyesight. In the last part of the year 1983 he had requested his son-in-law to assist him in his business
allowed_spans.reason: Tenant's competing explanation for the son-in-law's presence in the business.

allowed_spans.quote: A partnership deed dated 20.11.1983 (Ex.AW-3/13) has been executed between the father-in-law, Hakim Rai and his son-in-law, Raj Kumar to the aforenoted effect wherein the parties had agreed that the business under the said partnership would be conducted from the suit premises.
allowed_spans.reason: Documented existence and stated purpose of the partnership deed.

allowed_spans.quote: contention of the landlord, however, is that this partnership deed was a fake CM(M) No.1574/2010 Page 2 of 10 and forged document and had been created only as a sham defence to the present eviction petition under cite12†Section 14(1)(b) of the DRCA
allowed_spans.reason: Landlord's attack on the partnership deed as sham/fabricated.

allowed_spans.quote: she denied the CM(M) No.1574/2010 Page 4 of 10 suggestion that her husband was no longer in possession or in the business after the induction of Raj Kumar
allowed_spans.reason: Widow's testimony directly denies loss of the original tenant's possession/business role.

allowed_spans.quote: she had also admitted that Raj Kumar was partner in the business of her husband in the demised shop
allowed_spans.reason: Express admission of Raj Kumar's partnership role.

allowed_spans.quote: the son-in- law (Raj Kumar) and father-in-law (Hakim Rai) are residing in the same premises and ration card of Raj Kumar has been obtained at the same address. The partnership deed Ex.AW-3/13 had been executed between the parties in November, 1983
allowed_spans.reason: Recorded co-residence/ration-card fact and timing of the partnership deed.

allowed_spans.quote: The attorney of the landlord PW-3 has also admitted that the respondent Hakim Rai is an old man; he has very poor eyesight and cannot even walk properly.
allowed_spans.reason: Landlord-side admission supporting the defense explanation for reliance on the son-in-law.

cases.law_scope: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 14(1)(b), on fresh findings after remand; the earlier Section 14(1)(a) ground is outside the selected issue.
cases.target_stage: Fresh Section 14(1)(b) findings by the Additional Rent Controller after the RCT permitted additional evidence and remanded for fresh findings.
cases.target_court: Court of Sh. Ajay Nagar, Additional Rent Controller-02 (Central), Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi.
cases.substantive_issue: Whether the respondent had sublet, assigned, or otherwise parted with legal/physical possession of the shop to Kapil Luthra, and whether any written landlord consent existed, where the respondent characterized Kapil's presence as assistance in a family/partnership business.

issue_refs.quote: In view of provision of law, the landlord is required to prove following essential conditions:-
(i) The tenant sub-let, assigned or parted with the possession of the whole or part of the premises. i.e. the sub tenant was in exclusive possession of property or part of the property.
(ii). No consent in writing was taken from the landlord by the tenant.

application_refs.quote: As such, the respondent has admitted in reply to legal notice, the presence of Sh. Kapil Luthra at the tenanted premises but has claimed that he is merely helping the respondent and respondent is in possession of tenanted premises.

As such, the respondent clearly changed his stand in the testimony although respondent has claimed that he himself is running and managing the shop alongwith his nephew but perusal of record shows that he has been unable to prove this fact as no reliable cogent and convincing documentary or oral evidence has been placed on record by the respondent.
As such, the testimony of RW2 Sh. Kapil Luthra clearly shows that he has admitted that he is running the business in the tenanted premises and he does not have any other shop or other business.
Perusal of entire testimony of witnesses and material on record shows that respondent or his LR's are neither in physical possession nor in legal possession of the tenanted premises.
As such, in view of exhaustive discussion as earlier, this ingredient cite9†u/s 14 (1) (b) is satisfied.
Perusal of record shows that in the present petition, the respondent has not claimed in his written statement that the consent in writing was taken from the petitioner.
In view of the discussions, the petitioner has been able to prove all the ingredients of Sec. 14(1)(b) of D.R.C. Act against the respondent.

exclusive possession means the possession to the exclusion of others and it includes not only the physical possession but also the legal possession.

So long as the tenant keeps the control with him, it can not be said that sub-tenant is in exclusive possession of premises and in such situation the case does not fall within Section 14 (1)(b) D.R.C. Act.

"21. It is well settled that the burden of proving subletting is on the landlord but if the landlord proves that the subtenant is in exclusive possession of the suit premises, then the onus is shifted to the tenant to prove that it was not a case of subletting."
